newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt to cut import duties from July.
newsitem.headline: Egypt to cut import duties from July.

text.p: Egypt will cut import tariffs again from July as part of its economic liberalisation programme, an executive director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in an interview published on Sunday.
Abdel Shakour Shaalan, who represents Egypt and other Arab countries on the IMF board, told the government newspaper al-Ahram the amount of the reduction was up to the government.

"One of the achievements in the pipeline is the start of the second stage of trade liberalisation in July... The second stage will see further reductions in customs duties at a rate which the government will fix," he said.
Egypt last cut customs duties at the end of September last year, when the maximum for goods other than luxuries fell to 55 percent from 70 percent.
That reduction cleared the way for a new agreement with the IMF and persuaded Egypt's official creditors to waive loans to Egypt worth about $4 billion.
Shaalan said an IMF mission's second quarterly report on the Egyptian government's economic policy would go to the IMF board in the first week of July.
No finance is at stake but approval is important for Egypt's reputation among international investors.
Shaalan said the Egyptian government had given a commitment to privatise a certain number of large companies by the time of the board meeting but he did not give details.
"Under this new arrangement privatisation of most public-sector companies is expected to end by September 1998, the date for the end of the programme with the fund," he added.
Trade liberalisation has added to Egypt's import bill but there has been no corresponding increase in Egyptian exports.

Shaalan noted that many of the imports were capital goods for investment. "The trend towards imports is not worrying as long as it is for growth and as long as this coincides with an increase in exports," he added.
He said the government had removed many legal disincentives to investment but a change of mentality was still needed.
"We still need something deeper than measures. We need the spirit itself. We change the laws but the mentality which enforces them is still as it was," he said.
Shaalan said that in the coming year Egyptian money supply would grow more than 12 percent, from between 10 and 11 percent, because of a higher rate of economic growth.
The latest central bank figures show money supply grew 12.5 percent in the year to the end of February.
